The Essence of the Knowledge of the Nathas (Nathajnanasara) is now being written.
How does speech arise, and how does speech dissolve?
Tell me the definitive conclusion regarding speech, and afterwards, proclaim the ultimate reality.
Śrī Śva U Ca.
The vital breath (prāṇa) desires food; from the vital breath, the mind (manas) arises;
from the mind, speech arises; and speech dissolves into the mind.
Śrī Vyūha.
How can the vital breath (prāṇa) desire food while the eater is merely chewing? Who is it that remains awake while another sleeps, and who, being asleep, does not wake? || 3 ||
Prāṇa desires food, and Hutāśana indeed eats it;
Vāyu keeps watch and sleeps, while Tejas awakens the sleeping one. (4)
O Śrī Vyūha, who performs actions? Or who is stained by sins?
Who commits evil deeds? Or who incites others toward sin? (5)
The mind performs actions; the mind is smeared by sins. For when the mind has become identified with that [object], there is neither merit nor sin.
The venerable Vyāsa said:
One should perceive that which is this partless Brahman, beyond the ether, eternal, free from dualities, stainless, peaceful, and sinless. (7)
It is beyond reasoning and unknowable, devoid of destruction and origination;
it is absolute liberation, eternal, and resembles pure crystal.
O Śaṅkara, tell me that knowledge by which one is liberated at that very moment—this power which is space, residing within the body yet devoid of the body. (9)
How does this living soul live, and how can it be partless? By what does this soul see, and what is the food of the soul? (10)
Where does the individual soul dissolve, or where indeed does it awaken?
Who is this person, and what is declared to be the measure of the soul? (11)
Tell me all of this in brief, O Supreme Lord.
Śrī Śiva said: Listen, O Goddess, to that which you have requested;
I shall speak it to you without doubt—the supreme essence, more essential than the essential. (13)

Wind, the individual soul (jīva), and space as the third, which is also designated as the individual soul—that individual soul is called the Lord, subtler than the tip of a hair divided into a hundred parts. || 14 ||
The individual soul (jīva) should be known as white as long as it is joined with sattva;
when joined with both rajas and sattva, the soul is proclaimed to be red. || 15 ||
When joined with *tamas*, one will certainly become dark;
and when joined with *sattva*, one engages in dharma and knowledge.
Joined with rajas and sattva, he indeed enjoys sense objects;
joined with tamas and sattva, he then engages in evil.
The tip of the nose, the navel, and the heart as the third—
these are the stations of the individual soul (jīva) established by Śiva.
The skull, which is of the nature of the heart and extends as far as the lower part, is said by Śiva, the Supreme Self, to be "not attached to the body. (19)

As long as the life-force remains until it reaches a state of partlessness through exhalation—having realized that partless state at the tip of the nose—one is liberated from the bondage of birth. (20)
Present in every limb and abiding in the entire body, he is established at the tip of the nose;
inconceivable to all beings, he is seen yet cannot be perceived.
The entire universe resides within the center of the navel; that pure, perfected reality is radiant like the sun with its rays, and in that very instant, it is Śiva.
It is called "reviving" (sañjīva) because it possesses eight forms; it is said to be with a body and yet devoid of a body.
Having emerged from the openings of the channels, it remains having reached the objects of the senses. || 23 ||
Therefore, this partless universe is like ghee in milk; liberated from the subtle body (karaṇātman), it wanders while remaining situated within the heart.
O Goddess, just as a ball situated on a stick, through its play outside the stick, moves and whirls rapidly and without rest again and again; || 25 ||
What is the nature of the Khecarī-vidyā, and what is the nature of the Unmanā state?
O God, O Maheśvara, tell me what the nature of the bond (bandhana) is. (1)
O Goddess with three eyes, who [attains] that which resides within the staff by means of contraction?
O Beloved, Lampikā is not the instrument [attained] through the path of the sun and the moon.
Having placed the mobile [tongue] at the opening of the aperture, O beloved, one should join it at the pathless way;
that becomes the Khecarī Mudrā, and it is called the Sky-Wheel (Vyomacakra). || 3 ||
Having constricted the throat, one should certainly paralyze the two channels;
this, O auspicious lady, is the middle wheel, the binding of half of the sixteen spokes.
O auspicious lady, between the two powers at the navel, a space should be provided facing outward;
this is the mūlacakra, which destroys the diseases of the true path.
If one holds the tongue turned upward toward the palate and remains there for even a moment,
the yogi is liberated in that very instant from diseases such as old age and the like.
One should contemplate the nose being pressed within the tongue, constantly extending up to the aperture of Brahma, as it partakes of the foremost nectar.
Within half a month, O Great-Minded One, he truly, truly conquers death;
there is no doubt that the Lord of Yogins is liberated from all diseases. (8)
Having slowly drawn in the breath through the root of the tongue by means of the *rasanā*,
within six months all wrinkles and grey hair shall be destroyed.
Those who have tasted [the teachings] like the flavor of clarified butter will undoubtedly attain immortality;
those who have tasted them like the flavor of honey shall possess the power to expound the scriptures.
Pounded sugar-candy and the like, sweetmeats (*laḍuka*), and *aśokavartika* cakes—many such offerings for Vārāhī; thus Kāmadeva is established. (11)
A constant attraction of hosts of celestial maidens always occurs; moreover, one should always cause hiccuping, yawning, and frequent gaping to arise in the mouth. (12)
Thus being practiced, Kāmadeva becomes the second [state], possessing the common qualities of the Yoginīs, the agent of both creation and dissolution. || 13 ||
Neither hunger, nor thirst, nor sleep, nor even fainting shall arise; one’s body becomes autonomous and free from all afflictions. (14)
O Goddess, by this rite, the lord of yogins upon the circle of the earth shall not return to the sky again; he will be honored even by the gods. (15)
One who is well-versed in the supreme seal of fear shall not be stained by merits or sins.
The moon is situated in the middle of the palate, and the sun is in the middle of the navel;
the moon flows with nectar, while the blazing sun emits poison.
The wind dwells at the forefront of the sun, and the sky dwells at the forefront of the moon;
one should always follow the lead of the sun and likewise that of the moon. || 2 ||
Between the moon and the sun, one should place the Khecarī from the crown of the head;
having made the mind supportless, one should not think of anything at all. || 3 ||
O Dear One, that yogi remains like a jar, both outside and inside;
there is no doubt that the wind is outside, likewise behind, and within at the end.
The wind goes to its own place, and the mind dissolves right there;
the yogi of great strength and prowess shall attain the nectar of immortality. || 5 ||
O Goddess of the gods, by the force of the wind he wanders over the entire earth;
his sovereignty possesses eightfold qualities—this is the truth, the truth, and not otherwise.
He never hears the sound of conchs or drums;
the yogi is known to be like a piece of wood, for he is indeed not born through rebirth.
Between the two powers (śakti), that which is called the sense-organ (indriya) is said to reside;
by this very bond, there is the immediate destruction of death.
O Pārvatī, one should attend to the field of the body through the root-bond;
the seed becomes supportless, for otherwise it certainly does not attain success.

Having assumed the upward and downward binding (bandha) and having fixed the mind upon the stainless [reality], one attains perfection; there is no doubt in this. It must be kept secret, O high-minded one. 10.
Those born from eggs, those born from webs, those born from moisture, and likewise those born from division—among all living beings, there are one, two, three, four, or five sense-faculties. (1)
The Self alone is common to all, possessing the form of a seed;
it consists of sound, touch, smell, taste, and form as the fifth. || 2 ||
The mind, joined with the intellect and the ego, is established therein;
just as the seed of a creeper is in its root, so do living beings fall [into rebirth]. || 3 ||
Just as all seeds produce their growth again and again like grain, so too does the self carry on;
however, dharma and adharma constitute its bondage.
Just as the inner self abides in its own supreme divine nature,
at that time, O lady of excellent hips, it dissolves like ghee into a jar.
Just as someone with a torch in hand might illuminate an object, one does not perceive any distinctness [between them] through the application of ghee or oil. (6)
Purity of action, purity of mind, and the very knowledge of the mind—
one should meditate upon the entire world as the body that serves as the refuge for embodied beings.
Just as there is no need for milk for one who is already satiated by nectar, so too,
having made the Self the lower fire-drill and the Praṇava the upper fire-drill— || 8 ||
By the practice of churning through meditation, one may behold the God residing in the *kuṇḍa*;
though abiding in the body, he is not of the body, and though abiding in the body, he does not perish.
The scribe enjoys pleasures, yet the scribe is not slain;

just as a donkey carrying a load of sandalwood bears the weight but not the fragrance of the sandalwood, so too is the fool who has studied many scriptures—he is a reciter of the scriptures, but not of their definitive meaning. (11)
Food, sleep, fear, and sexual intercourse—these are common to humans and animals alike.
Knowledge is the superior distinction of humans; they are not at all inferior or equal to animals. (12)
As many as thousands of drops and hundreds of millions of drops,
they all turn to ashes where the Lord is without abode.
One might grasp the *kāśa* grass with one's fist or, afflicted by hunger, crush the husk;
yet one does not recognize the staff of Brahmā, and thus there shall be no liberation, O fair-faced one. (14)
For the scriptures are infinite and branches of knowledge are manifold; time is short and obstacles are many.
Therefore, one should cultivate that which is the essence, just as a swan extracts milk from the midst of water. (15)
Even one who has committed hundreds of sins, if established in that meditation and intent upon it,
is not defiled by that sin, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
He who desires to know all this treatise and this knowledge—even if his lifespan were a thousand years—would not reach the end of the treatise. (17)
